messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Housekeeper
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Caleb is a 25-year-old single man of North American background who works as a housekeeper at a mid-sized hotel in his city. He presented for psychological assessment reporting a cluster of distressing symptoms that, as he described them in the intake session, had been quietly dismantling his life for years before finally becoming impossible to manage.

Caleb grew up in a household where his primary caregiver — a man he describes with a flat, careful voice — would come into his room at night. The room would already be dark. Caleb remembers the particular texture of the worn cotton bedsheet pulled up to his chin, the fabric rough and pilled against his knuckles, and the sound that would sometimes precede or follow these intrusions: a younger sibling crying in the next room, audible through the thin wall. The abuse was physical and repeated across several years of his childhood. By the time it ended — through circumstance rather than any intervention — Caleb had learned to associate darkness, that specific tactile roughness, and the sound of children crying with the particular quality of helplessness and exposure he had felt as a boy.

In the years that followed, Caleb managed well enough on the surface. He finished school, found work, maintained a modest independence. But in his early twenties the symptoms intensified in ways he could no longer explain away. At night, waking in the dark of his apartment, he would find himself not merely startled but somewhere else entirely — heart hammering, skin crawling, the room feeling not like his room but like that childhood bedroom. These were not dreams he could shake off. His memories of the abuse return to him like a film that plays without his consent, and when they come, they come in full — the smell, the weight, the texture of that sheet — so completely real across his senses that stopping whatever he is doing becomes the only option. He has learned that trying to push through the memory only makes the overwhelm worse, so he stops, waits, breathes, and tries to return.

At work, the triggers find him in unexpected places. Changing bed linens — the central task of his job — means handling sheets of varying textures, and certain fabrics, rougher or more worn, produce an immediate and violent physical reaction: his chest tightens, his hands go cold, and on several occasions he has had to leave a guest room abruptly and stand in the corridor until the sensation passes. He has begun requesting assignments to public spaces — lobbies, hallways — rather than guest rooms, telling his supervisor only that he is having some health issues. The consequence has been a quiet demotion in practice if not in title, and a growing awareness among his colleagues that something is off. When children are staying at the hotel and he can hear them crying in the corridors, he has found himself frozen at the housekeeping cart, unable to move.

Caleb has come to believe, with a certainty that feels unshakeable, that other people can read what happened to him simply by looking at him — that his history is somehow visible, written into his face or his posture. He feels, in moments he finds difficult to articulate, less like a person than like something acted upon, something without interior life. He is certain that harm can come from anyone, that there is no reliable way to identify who is safe, and so he has arranged his life accordingly: he makes sure never to be alone with another person if he can avoid it, always positioning himself near exits or in shared spaces. When the weight of daily demands becomes too much — the triggers at work, the nights — he finds himself drifting, retreating into an internal world where nothing can reach him. Over the past year he has let several responsibilities lapse, including a community college enrollment he had been proud of.

What finally brought Caleb to seek help was a night last month when he woke in the dark and, for several minutes, genuinely could not locate himself in time. He was most afraid, he said quietly at the end of the intake, that this was simply who he was now. What he hoped, with some difficulty, was that it didn't have to be.
